HyperFrames renders HTML to video by seeking a paused timeline frame by frame, so every render is identical; the person edits the same files in the Studio preview. ## Contract

`npx hyperframes check --json` reports most violations with a `Fix:` line.

1. Every timed element has `class="clip"`, `data-start` and `data-duration` in seconds, and shows over `[start, start + duration)`: land an end state just before its end. `data-track-index` is only a Studio lane; paint order is `z-index`.
2. The video's length is the root's `data-duration`: overrun is cut, an early end holds the last frame.
3. Each composition builds one paused timeline and registers it after its tweens: `window.__timelines["<data-composition-id>"] = tl`.
4. No `Date.now()`, unseeded `Math.random()`, network fetches, timers or `repeat: -1`. Everything visible is a function of timeline time.
5. Never tween `display`, `visibility` or `autoAlpha` on a `.clip`; animate a child.
6. No CSS `transform` on an element GSAP transforms; animate transforms, not `left`/`top`/`width`/`height`.
7. Never `play()`, `pause()` or seek media. A `<video>` keeps its sound with `data-has-audio="true"`, else it is `muted`; music, voice, replacement sound and J/L cuts are a separate `<audio>`.
8. Every `<audio>` has an `id` or it is left out of the mix. No `crossorigin` on media. Time a `<video>` or its wrapper, never both.
9. Only the bundled fonts (`references/format.md`) resolve by name; any other family needs `@font-face` to a file in `assets/fonts/`.
10. Asset paths are root-relative (`assets/...`), in sub-compositions too.
11. Grades, grain, blur and vignettes on footage go through `npx hyperframes media-treatment` (`/media-use`), never CSS filters.
12. A scene file puts its styles, markup and scripts inside `<template>` and styles its root as `#root`. Intended overflow or overlap: `data-layout-allow-overflow`, `data-layout-allow-overlap`.

1: # Animation runtimes
2: 
3: HyperFrames seeks each frame on its own, so motion must be a function of time, never of the previous frame. Full GSAP reference: `npx hyperframes docs gsap`.
4: 
5: ## GSAP facts that bite
6: 
7: - Register the timeline last. Building inside `document.fonts.ready.then(…)` or another async callback is fine if you register at the end of it; registering first renders blank (`gsap_timeline_registered_before_async_build`).
8: - Place tweens at absolute seconds (`tl.to(el, {…}, 2.4)`). Set start states in the tween (`fromTo`), not in CSS.
9: - Measure layout once before building tweens, never inside `onUpdate`.
10: - Finite repeats only: `repeat: Math.max(0, Math.floor(duration / cycle) - 1)`.
11: - Seed randomness with a small PRNG (mulberry32).
12: - A scene's timeline can't reach elements outside its file, and two timelines must not animate the same property of one element.
13: - Transforms on a `<span>` need `display: inline-block` or `block`.
14: - Text that must fit a width: `window.__hyperframes.fitTextFontSize(text, { fontFamily, fontWeight, maxWidth })` returns `{ fontSize }`; `window.__hyperframes.pretext` measures text without a reflow.
15: 
16: ## Other runtimes
17: 
18: | Runtime                      | Use for                           | How HyperFrames drives it                                                                        |
19: | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
20: | CSS `@keyframes`             | Simple loops and decoration       | Found automatically; finite iterations, `animation-fill-mode: both`, `data-start` on the element |
21: | WAAPI                        | Native keyframes                  | `element.animate(…, { fill: "both" })` then `pause()`; times are document time, so use `delay`   |
22: | Lottie / dotLottie           | After Effects exports, characters | `autoplay: false`, always set `loop`, push the instance to `window.__hfLottie`                   |
23: | anime.js v4                  | Existing anime code               | `autoplay: false`, push to `window.__hfAnime`, `anime.createSeededRandom`                        |
24: | Three.js, WebGPU, p5, canvas | 3D and generative                 | Draw from `e.detail.time` in an `hf-seek` listener; set `data-duration` on the root              |
25: 
26: Charts and map overlays: drive them from a GSAP tween's `onUpdate`, not the library's own transitions. A real place is shown on baked imagery, not drawn (`film.md` "Maps and real places"). Heavy setup (big meshes, shader compiles) registers a `window.__hf.buildReady["<key>"]` promise.
27: 
28: ## The seek protocol
29: 
30: ```html
31: <script>
32:   function renderAt(t) {
33:     /* draw the frame for t seconds from state derived from t alone */
34:   }
35:   window.addEventListener("hf-seek", (e) => {
36:     renderAt(e.detail.time);
37:     // async work (GPU submit, image decode): e.detail.waitUntil(promise), called synchronously
38:   });
39:   renderAt(0);
40: </script>
41: ```
42: 
43: No `requestAnimationFrame` loop or timer as the clock.

Rendering

Render compositions to MP4 with npx hyperframes render.

Local Mode (default)

Uses Puppeteer (bundled Chromium) + system FFmpeg. Fast for iteration.
Requires: FFmpeg installed (brew install ffmpeg or apt install ffmpeg).

Docker Mode (--docker)

Deterministic output with exact Chrome version and fonts. For production.
Requires: Docker installed and running.

Options

  • -f, --fps — 24, 30, or 60 (default: 30)
  • -q, --quality — draft, standard, high (default: standard)
  • -w, --workers — Parallel workers 1-8 (default: auto)
  • --crf — Override encoder CRF (mutually exclusive with --video-bitrate)
  • --video-bitrate — Target video bitrate such as 10M (mutually exclusive with --crf)
  • --vp9-cpu-used — WebM VP9 speed/quality tradeoff (-8 to 8, default: 4). Higher values encode faster with larger output / quality tradeoff.
  • --video-frame-format — Source video frame extraction format: auto, jpg, or png (default: auto). Use png for UI recordings, screen captures, and color-sensitive source videos.
  • --gpu — Use GPU encoding (NVENC, VideoToolbox, AMF, VAAPI, QSV)
  • --browser-gpu / --no-browser-gpu — Force host GPU or software (SwiftShader) for Chrome/WebGL capture. Default for local renders is auto — probe WebGL availability on first launch and fall back to software if no GPU is reachable. Docker mode always uses software.
  • -o, --output — Custom output path

Tips

  • Use draft quality for fast previews during development
  • Local renders auto-detect GPU on first launch; use --browser-gpu to force hardware (errors if no GPU) or --no-browser-gpu to force SwiftShader
  • Use --gpu when a local render also benefits from hardware FFmpeg encoding
  • Use --video-frame-format png when source videos contain saturated UI colors that should avoid JPEG extraction
  • Use npx hyperframes benchmark to find optimal settings

2: 
3: You wrote the timeline, so you know what happens; the viewer sees it once, at full speed, often on a phone. Review is how you see the film as they will: as a harsh motion director, not a proud author. `check` catches what is broken; this pass catches what is weak. Run it after `check` passes, on every new film and on any edit that changes timing or layout, before you reply or render.
4: 
5: ## 1. Measure, then look
6: 
7: 1. `npx hyperframes check --json`. Besides errors it warns on craft it can measure: a line on screen too briefly to read (`line_unread`), more than 3 s with nothing changing (`dead_stretch`), text under 2.6% of the frame's short side (`text_below_floor`), an empty first frame (`first_frame_empty`, the thumbnail on social players), a film over 15 s with no sound (`film_silent`). A warning is a question, not a rule: fix it, or keep it on purpose and say why in the note (a deliberate hold carries `data-hold`).
8: 2. `npx hyperframes snapshot --review` writes three sheets: each scene just after it starts and at its middle, plus each `data-beat`, a strip across every cut (−0.2 s to +0.2 s), and the beat frames at phone width (360 px). Open all three.
9: 3. Motion between the beats: `snapshot --range START,END --frames 8` around the hero move and the payoff; `keyframes --shot` for a path that must arc or land.
10: 4. The rendered file: `npx hyperframes audio <video> --json` shows whether sound is there, where it hits and how loud it is. You cannot hear it; say so.
11: 
12: Trust the numbers over your eye where they disagree: a clipped label or a 0.6 s line looks fine on a contact sheet.
13: 
14: ## 2. What to look for
15: 
16: First, describe each beat frame in one sentence as a stranger would, naming every object; an object you would have to explain ("those bars are mirrors") is a P0. Then read the beat frames in order: do they tell a story a stranger follows, each one causing the next? Compare each with its shot in `SPEC.md`; what does not match is a note. Then name every default the frames show (`spec.md` "BANNED by default", or one not on the list yet), add each to the BANNED line, and fix them before anything else.
17:

20: | Question                      | What it catches                                                                                                                                    |
21: | ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
22: | Does it read as what it is?   | A shape that reads as another object, a material that reads as plastic, a product screen that reads as a mockup, a face or mascot that reads wrong |
23: | Does the subject separate?    | Subject and ground too close in value, two focal points in one frame, the eye with nowhere to go                                                   |
24: | Framing and contact           | Crops, text at the edge or under platform UI, collisions at a seam, things floating that should touch                                              |
